qs.q: Lead poisoning causes a porphyria-like syndrome by inhibiting
o: Inhibits porphobilinogen deaminase, causing an acute intermittent porphyria-like picture
Inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, causing ALA and zinc protoporphyrin accumulation
Inhibits uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase alone, causing severe cutaneous lesions
Inhibits ferrochelatase alone, causing protoporphyrin accumulation in red blood cells
qs.e: Lead inhibits two enzymes: ALA dehydratase (early in pathway) → ALA accumulates (similar to AIP — can cause abdominal pain + neurological features) AND ferrochelatase (late) → zinc incorporated instead of iron → elevated ZPP in RBCs (useful screening test). Also causes: microcytic anaemia (basophilic stippling), encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy (wrist/foot drop), renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome). Tre

ai.clinicalScope: Acute and chronic lead poisoning in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Lead Poisoning
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lead poisoning is systemic toxicity from absorbed lead, most often from occupational, environmental or contaminated food sources. It produces a characteristic microcytic anemia, neurocognitive decline and abdominal pain, with severity linked to blood lead level.

sections.p: Lead poisoning is the accumulation of lead in the body sufficient to cause clinical toxicity. Diagnosis rests on a raised blood lead level (BLL) together with compatible signs.
b: BLL ≥ 5 µg/dL in children or ≥ 10 µg/dL in adults is abnormal (WHO/CDC thresholds).
Confirm with a venous whole‑blood sample; capillary testing is acceptable only if confirmed by venous repeat.

sections.p: Severity is graded by BLL, which guides urgency of chelation and monitoring.
b: Mild: 5–44 µg/dL (children) / 10–44 µg/dL (adults) – monitor, remove source.
Moderate: 45–69 µg/dL – consider oral chelator (dimercaptosuccinic acid, DMSA).
Severe: ≥70 µg/dL – intravenous chelator (dimercaprol) plus supportive care.

sections.p: In East Africa, the most common sources are occupational exposure, contaminated traditional medicines, and lead‑laden dust from recycling or paint.
b: Occupational: battery manufacturing, metal smelting, mining.
Household: lead‑based paints, glazed pottery, contaminated water from leaded pipes.
Traditional remedies: herbal concoctions, kohl eye cosmetics.
Secondary: pica in iron‑deficient children leading to ingestion of lead‑containing soil.

sections.p: Presentation varies with age and BLL; children show neurodevelopmental regression, while adults often present with gastrointestinal and hematologic signs.
b: Abdominal colic (“lead colic”), constipation, nausea.
Micro‑cytic, hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling on smear.
Neurocognitive decline: irritability, attention deficit, seizures in severe cases.
Renal dysfunction: proteinuria, reduced GFR in chronic exposure.

sections.p: If BLL testing is unavailable, rely on clinical picture, basophilic stippling, and exclusion of other micro‑cytic anemias.

t.b: Quantifies exposure; determines severity and need for chelation.
Looks for basophilic stippling; supports diagnosis when BLL unavailable.

t.a: Complete blood count with iron studies
t.b: Identifies microcytic anemia; iron studies usually normal in lead poisoning.
Detects lead‑induced nephropathy; proteinuria signals chronic damage.
Assesses cognitive impact; guides need for rehabilitation.

sections.p: Prompt recognition of severe toxicity prevents irreversible damage.
b: BLL ≥ 70 µg/dL or encephalopathy (seizures, coma).
Severe anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL) with hemodynamic instability.
Acute renal failure (creatinine rise > 0.3 mg/dL).
Persistent abdominal pain unresponsive to analgesia.

sections.p: Remove source, provide chelation when indicated, and support affected organ systems.
b: Source control: stop exposure, educate family, replace leaded cookware.
Mild cases: dietary iron, calcium, and zinc supplementation to reduce absorption.
Moderate cases: oral DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) for 5‑14 days.
Severe cases: IV dimercaprol (British anti‑Lewisite) plus aggressive hydration.
Supportive: treat anemia with transfusion if symptomatic, manage pain, monitor renal function.

sections.p: Long‑term monitoring ensures reversal of toxicity and prevents re‑exposure.
b: Repeat BLL at 1, 3 and 6 months after chelation.
Screen household members, especially siblings and pregnant women.
Community education on safe storage of batteries and avoidance of leaded paints.
Implement routine screening in high‑risk schools.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause micro‑cytic anemia or abdominal pain.
b: Iron‑deficiency anemia – distinguished by low ferritin and response to iron; often co‑exists with lead exposure via pica.
Thalassaemia trait – micro‑cytosis with normal iron studies and target cells on smear.
Sideroblastic anemia – ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow; elevated ferritin.
Acute abdominal emergencies (appendicitis, malaria) – lack of basophilic stippling and normal BLL.
Capillary BLL may be falsely high due to skin contamination; confirm with venous sample.
Basophilic stippling can appear in severe anemia of other causes; always correlate with BLL.
Renal labs may be normal early; repeat if exposure persists.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling hemoglobin with hemodynamic compromise

faq.q: Why does lead cause basophilic stippling?
faq.a: Lead inhibits pyrimidine‑5‑nucleotidase, preventing degradation of ribosomal RNA, which appears as coarse basophilic granules.

faq.q: Can iron supplementation worsen lead poisoning?
faq.a: No; adequate iron reduces gastrointestinal lead absorption, so iron is given unless iron overload is present.

faq.q: Is chelation needed for a BLL of 30 µg/dL?
faq.a: In children, chelation is not routinely recommended at 30 µg/dL; focus on source removal and nutritional measures.

exam: What bedside clues would make you suspect lead poisoning in a child with abdominal pain? — Look for pica, anemia with basophilic stippling, and a history of exposure to paint or traditional medicines.
How do you stage severity of lead poisoning and why does it matter? — Use blood lead level thresholds (mild 5‑44, moderate 45‑69, severe ≥70 µg/dL) to decide on chelation and monitoring intensity.
A patient presents with micro‑cytic anemia, normal ferritin, and abdominal colic. What is your next diagnostic step? — Order a venous blood lead level; a high result confirms lead toxicity.

When is intravenous dimercaprol indicated, and what are its key monitoring points? — Indicated for BLL ≥70 µg/dL or encephalopathy; monitor blood pressure, renal function, and for signs of hypertension.

Explain why iron deficiency can both mask and precipitate lead poisoning. — Iron deficiency increases gut lead absorption and may cause pica, yet low ferritin can mislead clinicians away from lead as a cause of anemia.

What public‑health measures would you recommend to a rural community with frequent cases of lead poisoning? — Remove leaded paint, educate on safe battery recycling, provide iron‑rich diet, and establish school‑based BLL screening.

How would you differentiate lead colic from malaria‑related abdominal pain in a febrile child? — Lead colic lacks fever, shows basophilic stippling and normal malaria smear; malaria shows parasites on thick smear and responds to antimalarials.

A pregnant woman has a BLL of 12 µg/dL. What counseling do you give? — Advise strict avoidance of lead sources, iron supplementation, and repeat testing in the third trimester to protect fetal neurodevelopment.
